messages.content: I want to design a typed language that supports multi-shot continuations and deterministic resource cleanup. The challenge is to allow repeated resumptions that are resource-safe, without duplicating ownership or invalidating computations that are resumed. The design should establish type safety and exactly-once cleanup for owned resources, and pass 30 conformance cases covering nested capture, repeated resumption, cancellation, and rejected ownership violations.

The central tension is that a multi-shot continuation can be resumed more than once, while an owned resource must not silently acquire multiple owners. Supporting both means the language cannot treat repeated resumption as permission to duplicate everything captured by a computation. It needs an account of which state can safely participate in repeated resumptions, what remains uniquely owned, and how cleanup occurs when a computation finishes or is cancelled.

Those are design and validation goals, not results already established. In particular, passing 30 conformance cases and demonstrating type safety and exactly-once cleanup would require a concrete language design and a way to check its behavior.
What does “resource-safe repeated resumptions” require beyond simply letting a continuation run twice?

Running twice is only the control-flow part. Resource safety also asks what each run is allowed to use. If a captured computation refers to an owned resource, resuming the continuation repeatedly must not give each run an independent claim to that same ownership. Nor can one run dispose of a resource in a way that leaves another resumed computation with an apparently valid but unusable reference.

At the level of the goal, repeated resumption must be accepted when it is safe, while ownership violations must be rejected. That avoids solving the problem by prohibiting all repeated resumptions: multi-shot behavior is an explicit part of what the language is meant to support.
So the typing question is not just whether a continuation has an input and output type?

Right. Input and output types alone do not express whether resuming it again would reuse an exclusive claim to a resource. A type-safety account for this goal would have to cover both ordinary computation and the ownership constraints associated with capture and resumption. It should explain why accepted programs cannot turn repeated control flow into duplicated ownership or leave a resumed computation relying on ownership that is no longer valid.

That describes what the account must establish; it does not prescribe a particular type system or proof technique.
How should I read “exactly-once cleanup” when a continuation can be resumed multiple times?

It is a claim about each owned resource, not a claim that cleanup should happen once per resumption regardless of ownership. Repeating a computation must not cause two cleanups of one owned resource, and cancellation or another permitted exit must not cause its cleanup to be skipped. Conversely, if there are distinct owned resources, each has its own cleanup obligation.

The difficult part is defining those obligations coherently when control can be captured, resumed, or cancelled. The language design needs to make the cleanup behavior deterministic without treating copies of control flow as copies of ownership.
Could a design meet the cleanup condition by rejecting every continuation that mentions an owned resource?

That might avoid some unsafe situations, but it would not by itself express the full goal. The requirement is to accept resource-safe repeated resumptions, not merely reject potential trouble. A useful design must distinguish cases that can safely be resumed repeatedly from cases that would duplicate ownership or otherwise invalidate a resumed computation.

The node does not specify where that boundary falls. Establishing and testing the boundary is part of the design problem.
I also want to be clear about cancellation. Is it just another way a continuation stops?

For this goal, cancellation matters because an owned resource may still have a cleanup obligation when a computation does not proceed to ordinary completion. The design must make that obligation predictable and avoid both omission and repetition. It also needs to keep cancellation from making any computation that may still be resumed appear to own a resource that has already been cleaned up.

That does not assume a particular cancellation mechanism. It states the safety questions the mechanism would need to answer.
And nested capture makes those questions harder?

Potentially, yes. With nested capture, more than one captured control context may be involved, so it is important to know which context is entitled to use an owned resource and when its cleanup obligation is discharged. Repeated resumption and cancellation can interact with that nesting. The goal therefore explicitly calls for conformance cases covering nested capture, rather than checking only a single, uncomplicated capture.
Would you describe the 30 cases as a proof of type safety?

No. Passing 30 conformance cases is a concrete validation requirement, while establishing type safety is a separate requirement. Tests can exercise expected acceptance, rejection, and cleanup behavior, including the named areas of nested capture, repeated resumption, cancellation, and rejected ownership violations. They cannot, solely by being 30 cases, establish a general theorem about every well-typed program.

Both forms of evidence matter to the stated goal, but neither should be represented as already complete.
Do the requirements specify how many of those cases belong to each area?

No. They specify 30 conformance cases in total and identify the areas those cases must cover, but they do not allocate a number to nested capture, repeated resumption, cancellation, or rejected ownership violations. Assigning counts within those areas would add a detail that is not part of the stated requirements.
What should a rejected ownership violation demonstrate, conceptually?

It should show that the language does not accept a program whose continuation use would violate ownership—for example, by giving repeated resumptions incompatible claims to the same owned resource. The precise program and rejection rule depend on the eventual design. Conceptually, the important point is that an unsafe use is rejected for an ownership reason, rather than being accepted with cleanup left ambiguous or a resumed computation left invalid.
Then the accepted cases should show the other side of the boundary?

Yes. Acceptance matters because the target is a typed language with genuine multi-shot continuations, including resource-safe repeated resumptions. The conformance cases should exercise that capability as well as the rejection of ownership violations. A design that rejects every repeated resumption could avoid some hazards, but it would not meet the stated acceptance requirement.
I keep coming back to the difference between repeating control flow and repeating ownership.

That distinction is the heart of it. A continuation describes computation that may be resumed again; an ownership claim governs who may use an owned resource and who is responsible for its cleanup. The design has to permit repeated control flow where safe without inferring that every captured ownership claim can also be repeated. Otherwise one resumption could clean up a resource another resumption still expects to use, or multiple resumptions could each attempt to clean up the same resource.

A sound account would make that distinction visible in what programs are accepted and in what happens when accepted programs complete or are cancelled.
Can we state the objective without choosing a particular implementation yet?

Yes: design a typed language that supports multi-shot continuations and deterministic cleanup; accepts repeated resumptions when they are resource-safe; prevents ownership from being duplicated and prevents resumed computations from being invalidated; establishes type safety and exactly-once cleanup for owned resources; and passes 30 conformance cases spanning nested capture, repeated resumption, cancellation, and rejected ownership violations.

That states the required behavior and evidence without claiming a particular mechanism, a completed proof, or completed test results.
Does deterministic cleanup mean the resource is necessarily cleaned up at the first resumption’s end?

Not necessarily. The stated goal does not assign a cleanup point to the first resumption. It requires a deterministic account that is consistent with ownership and exactly-once cleanup. In a multi-shot setting, assuming that the first run’s end always discharges a resource’s obligation could conflict with another permitted resumption. The design has to specify when cleanup is owed without creating that conflict.
So any proposal should be judged both on what it allows and on what it rules out?

Exactly. It must allow resource-safe repeated resumptions, while ruling out uses that duplicate ownership or invalidate resumed computations. It must also account for cleanup on the paths the language permits, including cancellation, so that each owned resource is cleaned up exactly once. The 30 conformance cases are a stated check on those behaviors across the specified categories; type safety remains an additional obligation to establish.

Here is a proposal for the ownership problem: grade continuations by ownership. Multi-shot resumptions would replay copyable frames that use handler-scoped borrows, while linear owners would be finalized on handler exit or cancellation.

That separates two things that repeated resumption might otherwise conflate: replaying a computation and copying ownership. Under the proposal, the portion replayed by a multi-shot continuation is copyable; access to a resource through a handler-scoped borrow does not give each replay its own ownership claim. The linear owner remains subject to finalization when the handler exits or is cancelled.

This is a proposed way to address the goal, not yet an established type-safety or exactly-once-cleanup result. Its key obligations are to define the ownership grades precisely, keep borrows within their handler scope, and make finalization consistent with every permitted resumption.
When you say the continuation is graded, is the grade about how many times it has already run?

Not in this proposal. “Graded by ownership” concerns what the continuation may retain and replay, rather than a count of past resumptions. A continuation eligible for multi-shot use must have replayable frames; it cannot obtain that eligibility by making additional owners out of a linear resource. The proposal does not specify particular grade names or a notation for them.
What exactly gets replayed when the continuation is resumed again?

The proposal identifies copyable frames as the part that can be replayed. A frame may use a handler-scoped borrow, but replaying that frame does not copy the linear owner behind the borrow. That distinction is what lets repeated computation remain possible without treating an exclusive resource as though it had become freely duplicable.

The exact representation of a frame, and the precise typing rules for deciding whether it is copyable, remain to be worked out.
Why specify that the borrows are handler-scoped?

Because a replay that relies on a borrow has to remain within the period when that borrow is valid. If the handler has exited or been cancelled and the linear owner is finalized, a resumed computation cannot safely continue using a borrow to that owner. Tying the borrow to the handler scope expresses the boundary the proposal needs: multi-shot replay may use borrowed access while that scope permits it, but the borrow cannot be treated as an enduring ownership claim.
Does that mean a borrow is another kind of copyable owner?

No. The point of the borrow is access without ownership duplication. Replaying a copyable frame that uses a handler-scoped borrow must not manufacture another linear owner or another independent cleanup obligation. Otherwise the proposal would merely disguise the ownership violation it is meant to prevent.
I'm concerned about a continuation that has been captured but has not yet been resumed when cancellation happens.

That is an important case for the proposal. Cancellation is one of the stated finalization events for linear owners. If cancellation finalizes an owner, a continuation whose replay would require a borrow of that owner must not subsequently be usable in a way that treats the borrow as valid. The eventual rules need to make that restriction clear, while still accepting repeated resumptions that are resource-safe. The proposal identifies the intended boundary; it does not yet specify how that boundary is enforced.
And if a handler exits normally instead of being cancelled?

Handler exit is the other stated finalization point for linear owners. The same scope issue applies: a borrow used by a replayable frame cannot remain valid after the handler scope that supports it has ended. Normal exit and cancellation both have to be accounted for without skipping cleanup or cleaning up the same owner twice.
Are you saying every resumption performs finalization?

No. Repeated resumption replays copyable frames; it does not create a new linear owner to finalize on every replay. The proposal places finalization of linear owners at handler exit or cancellation. Exactly-once cleanup is still an obligation to establish for that arrangement, especially where repeated resumptions and termination interact.
Could we simply mark any continuation that encounters a linear owner as single-shot?

The proposal is more discriminating than that. Its multi-shot path replays copyable frames with handler-scoped borrows while keeping linear ownership separate. Merely encountering borrowed access to a linear owner need not, by itself, imply that replay copies that owner. At the same time, a continuation must not be classified as safely multi-shot if replay would duplicate a linear ownership claim. The typing rules would need to distinguish those cases.
How does this help with nested capture?

Nested capture tests whether the same distinction remains clear across more than one captured context. For each multi-shot replay, the relevant frames still need to be copyable, and any borrowed access must stay within its handler scope. Linear owners must retain an unambiguous finalization obligation rather than being implicitly duplicated by the nesting. That explains why nested capture belongs among the conformance cases, without assuming the proposal has already passed them.
Would a type-safety argument only have to show that a repeated resumption is allowed by its grade?

That would be insufficient. The argument would also have to show that the grade is respected as computation proceeds: replay does not duplicate linear ownership, handler-scoped borrows are not used outside their valid scope, and a permitted resumption is not invalidated by cleanup. The separate exactly-once-cleanup obligation would need to account for finalization on handler exit or cancellation. None of those properties follows just from assigning a grade name.
What should the rejected ownership-violation cases test under this proposal?

They should probe attempts to use multi-shot replay as though it copied a linear owner, or to rely on a handler-scoped borrow where that scope no longer permits access. Rejection would demonstrate the intended ownership boundary; accepted cases would need to demonstrate that the boundary still permits resource-safe repeated resumptions. Those are conceptual targets for the cases, not claims that any particular cases have been written or passed.
Does the proposal change the target of 30 conformance cases?

No. The target remains 30 conformance cases covering nested capture, repeated resumption, cancellation, and rejected ownership violations. Grading continuations, replaying copyable frames with handler-scoped borrows, and finalizing linear owners on handler exit or cancellation are proposed design choices to examine against that target. The count and the required coverage do not change.
Let me check the core claim: the computation may be replayed, but its resource owner is not replayed with it.

Yes—that captures the intended separation. Multi-shot resumption replays copyable frames; handler-scoped borrows can provide access without becoming duplicate owners. The linear owner has its own finalization obligation on handler exit or cancellation. To turn that idea into a sound language design, the rules still have to ensure that every permitted replay has valid access and that each owned resource is cleaned up exactly once.
What static rule prevents captured handler-scoped borrows from outliving their owners during nested resumption or cancellation?

The needed rule is a borrow-escape restriction: a continuation that captures a handler-scoped borrow may be resumed only while that handler scope, and the owner supporting the borrow, remain live. Capturing the continuation must not make the borrow valid for longer. If resumption could occur after the scope ends or the owner is finalized, the program must be rejected or otherwise made unable to perform that resumption.

That describes the safety condition a static rule must enforce, not a typing rule that has already been specified and proved sufficient.
Is it enough to say that the continuation was captured inside the handler?

No. The place where it was captured does not, by itself, constrain where or when it can later be resumed. The static check has to account for the continuation after capture, including whether a reference to it can remain usable beyond the handler scope. Otherwise a borrow could be valid at capture time but invalid at resumption time.
How should the restriction carry through a second capture nested inside the first?

Nested capture cannot extend the lifetime of a borrow inherited from an outer captured context. If the inner continuation depends on that borrow, its permitted resumptions must remain within the borrow’s valid handler scope as well. More generally, every handler-scoped borrow needed by the resumed computation imposes a boundary; nesting does not erase an outer boundary or create a new owner.
Would checking only the innermost handler miss something, then?

It could. An inner continuation may still depend on a borrow associated with an enclosing handler. Its immediate capture site would not tell the whole story. The relevant question is whether every borrow on which a possible resumption depends will still have a live owner at that resumption. A static rule must retain those dependencies through nested capture rather than checking only the nearest scope.
What changes when cancellation can finalize the owner before a stored continuation is resumed?

Cancellation makes the boundary especially important. If cancelling the handler finalizes its linear owner, a stored continuation that depends on a borrow of that owner cannot remain usable for a later resumption. A static discipline would have to ensure that no such usable continuation survives the cancellation path, or reject a program in which it might. Merely recording that the borrow began inside the handler would not address that path.
Does that mean cancellation has to search for every captured continuation?

Not necessarily. That is one possible implementation question, but it is not what the static safety condition requires. The condition is that cancellation cannot leave a permitted resumption that uses a borrow whose owner has been finalized. A language could try to establish that through restrictions on where continuations may remain usable, through an account of their dependencies, or through some other precisely specified mechanism. The question here does not settle which mechanism to use.
I want repeated resumptions to remain possible. Would this rule accidentally make every borrow-dependent continuation single-shot?

It need not. The restriction is on the validity of borrowed access, not inherently on the number of resumptions. Repeatedly replaying copyable frames can be resource-safe while the relevant handler scope and owner remain live. What must be ruled out is a resumption after that access ceases to be valid, or a resumption that treats borrowed access as duplicated ownership.
But if the continuation can be copied, couldn't a copy be hidden somewhere until after cancellation?

That is exactly why an escape restriction has to cover every usable copy, not just the original continuation value. Allowing multi-shot use cannot also allow an unrestricted copy to retain authority to use a handler-scoped borrow after cancellation. If the static account cannot show that all possible resumptions remain inside the valid scope, it cannot justify accepting that use as resource-safe.
So a rule about the borrow's scope also has to constrain continuation values?

Yes. Once a continuation captures a borrow, the continuation carries a dependency on that borrow’s validity. Checking the borrow only at the point of capture is insufficient; the dependency matters wherever the continuation may be retained, copied, or resumed. In a nested case, a continuation can carry dependencies inherited through more than one captured context.
Could the rule instead allow a resumption after cancellation but promise that the borrowed resource won't be touched?

Only if the language can establish that the resumed computation does not rely on the invalid borrow. A blanket promise would not be enough for a continuation that still needs it. The essential static question is whether the particular permitted resumption can use an owner that has already been finalized. If it can, the rule has not prevented the lifetime violation.
Is this just an exactly-once-cleanup issue?

It is related but distinct. The owner might be cleaned up exactly once on cancellation, yet a later resumption could still try to use a borrow to that finalized owner. That would violate the validity of the resumed computation even without a second cleanup. Conversely, preventing the later use does not alone establish that cleanup occurs exactly once. The design needs both properties.
Can the rule be stated without deciding how continuation dependencies are represented in types?

Yes. A concise obligation is: any continuation permitted to resume using a handler-scoped borrow must remain confined to the period in which that borrow’s owner is live; nested capture preserves that obligation, and handler exit or cancellation cannot leave a usable, borrow-dependent resumption behind. The eventual static rules would need to express and enforce that obligation, including for repeated resumptions, without turning a borrow into another owner.
I have a hypothesis about the static boundary: if captured borrows cannot outlive handler regions, then resource-safe nested resumptions type-check, and cancellation leaves no dangling continuations.

That is a useful conditional hypothesis, but its two consequences still need to be established. The first says that confining captured borrows to their handler regions is not merely restrictive: it still permits nested resumptions when those resumptions are resource-safe. The second says that cancellation cannot leave a continuation usable in a way that depends on a borrow whose handler region has ended.

Neither consequence follows just from stating a lifetime restriction. The eventual rules would need to show how the restriction applies through capture, nesting, resumption, and cancellation.
When I say “captured borrows cannot outlive handler regions,” should that apply to the continuation value or only to an attempted use of the borrow?

The hypothesis needs a boundary strong enough to prevent an invalid later resumption. If a continuation remains usable after the handler region ends and resuming it can use a captured borrow, then merely prohibiting direct use of the borrow elsewhere would not suffice. The relevant lifetime dependency has to remain attached to the possibility of resuming that continuation.

That does not settle how a language represents the dependency. It identifies what the proposed restriction must prevent.
Why is nested resumption singled out in the hypothesis?

Nesting tests whether the restriction remains effective when a continuation captured within one control context is involved in another capture or resumption. A borrow from a handler region must not acquire a longer lifetime simply because the control flow is nested. At the same time, the hypothesis predicts that nested resumptions which stay resource-safe would still type-check. Both sides matter: preserving the boundary and accepting permitted uses.
Would it be accurate to paraphrase the first consequence as “all nested resumptions type-check”?

No. The hypothesis says *resource-safe* nested resumptions type-check. A nested resumption that would use a captured borrow beyond its handler region is outside that condition. Removing “resource-safe” would turn a qualified prediction into a much broader claim.
And does “cancellation leaves no dangling continuations” mean cancellation destroys every continuation?

Not necessarily. In this hypothesis, the concern is a continuation whose resumption would rely on a captured borrow after the handler region supporting that borrow has ended. “No dangling continuations” should be read in relation to that invalid dependency, not as a claim that cancellation eliminates all continuation values regardless of what they capture.
Suppose a nested continuation has been captured but not resumed before cancellation. What would the hypothesis predict?

If that continuation depends on a borrow confined to the cancelled handler region, the hypothesis predicts that cancellation does not leave it available for a later, invalid resumption. If its use does not depend on such an expired borrow, that particular dangling-borrow concern does not arise. The distinction depends on what the continuation may use, not simply on whether it was resumed before cancellation.
Is preventing an escape enough to show the nested resumption part?

Not on its own. Preventing a captured borrow from outliving its handler region addresses invalid access, but the hypothesis also predicts acceptance of resource-safe nested resumptions. To support that prediction, the static rules would have to recognize safe uses as well as exclude unsafe ones. Otherwise a rule that rejected every nested resumption might satisfy a narrow non-escape condition while failing the acceptance part of the hypothesis.
How does repeated resumption fit into this conditional claim?

A captured borrow’s region boundary must continue to hold across each permitted resumption. Repetition cannot extend the handler region or turn the borrow into ownership. The hypothesis can accommodate repeated nested resumptions when they remain resource-safe, but it does not claim that any number of resumptions is safe regardless of when they occur.
Could one successful resumption make a later one safe even after the handler region ends?

The earlier resumption would not, by itself, extend the captured borrow’s validity. If a later resumption still relies on that borrow after the handler region ends, it presents the same lifetime problem. The hypothesis rests on keeping permitted uses within the region, including later uses of a multi-shot continuation.
I want to avoid treating this as a completed result. What would need checking?

The proposed static restriction would need to be stated precisely enough to follow captured borrow dependencies through nested continuations. Then one would need to establish both predictions: resource-safe nested resumptions are accepted by the typing rules, and cancellation cannot leave a usable continuation with a borrow that has outlived its handler region. Until that work is done, these remain consequences the hypothesis proposes, not demonstrated properties.
Does the hypothesis by itself establish exactly-once cleanup for the owners?

No. Preventing dangling borrow-dependent continuations addresses whether a resumed computation can refer to an owner beyond the borrow’s valid region. Exactly-once cleanup also requires an account of whether and when each owned resource is finalized, without omission or duplication. The lifetime hypothesis is relevant to that broader goal, but it does not alone prove the cleanup property.
Then the core prediction is that the region limit can be strict without ruling out the safe nested cases?

Yes. The hypothesis is that confining captured borrows to their handler regions can do both jobs: permit resource-safe nested resumptions to type-check and ensure that cancellation leaves no dangling continuation dependent on an expired borrow. It remains a hypothesis until the static rules and their consequences are worked out.

I want to turn the borrow-lifetime question into a concrete plan: define region-indexed continuation typing, prove borrow nonescape across nested resumptions, and run 30 ownership, cleanup, and cancellation tests.

That plan has three distinct parts. Region-indexed continuation typing would make a continuation’s dependence on a handler region visible to the static rules. A borrow-nonescape proof would then need to show that nested capture and resumption cannot turn a borrow confined to that region into access beyond it. The 30 tests would exercise ownership, cleanup, and cancellation behavior.

These are planned steps, not completed definitions, proofs, or test results. The region-indexed typing rules in particular still need to say what a continuation may capture and where it may be resumed.
What work is the region index supposed to do?

Conceptually, it records a scope constraint that matters when a continuation captures a borrow. A continuation depending on a borrow from a handler region cannot be treated as usable without regard to that region. The index would give the typing rules a way to carry that constraint through capture and subsequent resumptions.

Calling the typing “region-indexed” does not yet specify its notation, the exact form of a continuation type, or every rule for combining regions.
Why put the region on continuation typing instead of checking the borrow only where it is first captured?

Because capture is not the last time the borrow matters. A continuation may be retained and resumed later, and nested resumption may carry the dependency into another captured computation. A check at the original capture site could find the borrow valid at that moment without establishing that it remains valid whenever the continuation is used. Region-indexed continuation typing is the planned way to keep that lifetime constraint in view.
Does the plan require me to prohibit nested resumptions?

No. It specifically calls for proving borrow nonescape *across nested resumptions*. The aim is to account for nesting while preventing borrowed access from outliving its handler region, not to avoid the issue by declaring all nested resumptions impermissible. The precise boundary between permitted and rejected uses would follow from the rules you define.
What would the nonescape proof have to rule out?

It would have to rule out a path where a continuation captures a handler-scoped borrow, nested resumptions carry that dependency forward, and a permitted use of the continuation accesses the borrow after its region has ended. Nesting must not silently lengthen the borrow’s lifetime. The proof would concern all resumptions allowed by the proposed typing rules, rather than only the first resumption or only a direct, unnested capture.
Is proving nonescape the same thing as proving that every resource is cleaned up exactly once?

No. Nonescape addresses whether a captured borrow can be used outside its valid region. Exactly-once cleanup addresses the finalization of owned resources: neither omitting cleanup nor doing it twice. The questions interact—cleanup must not leave a permitted continuation with invalid borrowed access—but a nonescape proof alone would not settle every cleanup obligation. That is one reason the plan also includes cleanup tests.
How should cancellation appear in the typing and proof work?

It must be treated as a possible end to a handler region when considering whether a captured borrow remains usable. The typing rules and nonescape argument need to prevent nested resumptions from retaining valid-looking borrowed access beyond that boundary. The cancellation tests would then exercise the corresponding behavior. The plan does not yet choose a particular mechanism for cancelling continuations or finalizing owners.
Could the 30 tests replace the proof if they include difficult nested cases?

No. Tests can check selected ownership, cleanup, and cancellation cases, including difficult ones, but they do not establish borrow nonescape for every program admitted by the typing rules. Conversely, a proof of nonescape would not make the planned tests unnecessary: the tests can check whether the defined language behaves as intended in concrete cases. The plan calls for both kinds of work.
Are those 30 tests already divided into fixed numbers for ownership, cleanup, and cancellation?

The plan gives a total of 30 tests and names ownership, cleanup, and cancellation as the areas to run them against. It does not specify a numerical split among those areas. Assigning one now would be an additional planning decision, not something already stated.
Should the ownership tests include rejected programs as well as accepted ones?

That would address both sides of the ownership question: whether safe uses are allowed and whether ownership violations are rejected. The plan itself does not enumerate individual tests, so it would be premature to claim a particular mix has been selected. Whatever cases are chosen should make their expected ownership behavior clear enough to evaluate.
What distinction should the cleanup tests keep in view?

They should keep separate the number of times computation is resumed and the number of ownership obligations. Replaying a computation does not by itself create another owner entitled to, or requiring, cleanup. Cleanup tests can examine whether owned resources are finalized as intended, including when execution does not reach an ordinary exit. The precise cases and expected outcomes still need to be specified before the tests can be run.
Would a passing cancellation test establish that no borrow can ever escape?

No. It would establish that the tested cancellation scenario behaved as expected. The planned borrow-nonescape proof is what would need to justify the general claim across nested resumptions admitted by the typing rules. Tests can reveal errors or provide concrete checks, but a finite set of 30 does not cover every possible captured continuation.
What would count as finishing the first step of the plan?

The first step would require an actual definition of region-indexed continuation typing, not just the phrase. It would need to make clear how a captured borrow’s region constrains a continuation’s permitted uses, including nested capture and resumption, so that a nonescape statement can be formulated against those rules. That is a description of the work to do, not a claim that the definition already exists.
And the proof comes after there is a rule precise enough to reason about?

Yes. To prove borrow nonescape, there must be a precise account of what is well typed and what nested resumptions are permitted. The proof obligation would then connect that static account to the lifetime claim: permitted resumptions cannot use a captured borrow outside its handler region. Without the defined rules, the intended property can be stated, but not established for this language.
I don't want the testing step to be mistaken for results. How would you phrase its status?

“Run 30 ownership, cleanup, and cancellation tests” is a planned activity. It does not say that the cases have been written, executed, or passed. Similarly, “prove borrow nonescape” names an intended proof obligation, not an already proved theorem. The immediate task is to make the region-indexed typing precise enough for both that proof and the planned tests.
I’m moving to the concrete activity: implement a region-indexed type checker and run 30 ContinuationSafe cases tracing borrow lifetimes, nested resumes, cancellation, and destructor counts.

That makes the lifetime question checkable in two complementary ways. The region-indexed type checker must determine whether a continuation’s captured borrows remain valid wherever it can be resumed, including through nesting. The 30 ContinuationSafe cases can then exercise those decisions and trace what happens to borrowed access and owned resources during resumption and cancellation.

This describes the activity to carry out; it does not imply that the checker is implemented or that any of the 30 cases have run or passed.
What should the checker keep track of when a continuation captures a borrow?

It needs to retain the continuation’s dependence on the borrow’s handler region. Otherwise, a later check might see a continuation value without seeing the lifetime constraint that comes with resuming it. The exact representation is an implementation choice, but the essential question is whether every permitted resumption occurs while the borrowed access is still valid.
Does that dependency still matter if the continuation is captured again inside another continuation?

Yes. Nested capture must not erase an existing region constraint. If resuming the inner continuation can reach computation that uses a borrow from an enclosing handler region, the checker still needs to account for that enclosing region. Checking only the innermost capture would leave the original lifetime question unanswered.
What should I look for in the borrow-lifetime traces?

Look for the relationship between a borrow’s valid handler region and each point at which a resumed computation may use it. A trace is useful if it makes clear whether nested resumes stay within that boundary and whether handler exit or cancellation precedes any attempted use. The trace can illustrate what happened in a case; the checker’s rules must still justify which cases are accepted or rejected.
Why trace nested resumes separately from borrow lifetimes?

They answer related but different questions. A nested-resume trace shows the control-flow situations the case exercises. A borrow-lifetime trace shows whether borrowed access remains within its valid region during those situations. Seeing both helps distinguish a case that genuinely exercises nested resumption from one that merely has a borrow, and helps identify where a lifetime violation would arise.
How does cancellation enter the checker’s decision?

Cancellation matters because it can end the handler region on which a captured borrow depends. The checker must not permit a continuation to remain usable for a resumption that would rely on that borrow after the region ends. The ContinuationSafe cancellation cases can exercise that boundary, but observing a few cases cannot substitute for a general static rule.
And why record destructor counts as well as cancellation?

A cancellation trace can show which path execution took; a destructor count addresses the separate cleanup obligation for an owned resource. The intended property is exactly-once cleanup for each owner, not one destructor call per resumption. Counts can reveal a missed cleanup or duplicate cleanup in a tested case, including a cancellation case, without by themselves proving the property for every program.
So repeated resumes shouldn’t automatically increase the destructor count for one owner?

Correct. Replaying computation is not the same as creating another linear owner. For a given owned resource, the cleanup obligation remains exactly once. The cases should make it possible to inspect whether repeated resumes have accidentally been treated as repeated ownership; no particular destructor count has yet been observed.
Could a case show a correct destructor count but still have an unsafe borrow?

Yes. An owner could be finalized once, while a later resumption still attempts to use a captured borrow after its handler region ends. That would be a lifetime problem despite the cleanup count. This is why the activity traces borrow lifetimes as well as destructor counts.

I propose combining ranked suspended handles, active-resumption guards, and owner-handle-free finalizers to support multi-shot borrows with deferred exactly-once cleanup.

The three parts address different pressures on resource lifetime. Ranked suspended handles constrain dependencies associated with continuations that may resume later. Active-resumption guards protect borrows while resumed computation is running. Owner-handle-free finalizers avoid making cleanup depend on a guarded handle to the very owner being finalized. Together, they offer a proposed way to repeat borrowed computation while keeping ownership singular and deferring cleanup until it can occur safely exactly once. This is a design proposal, not, by itself, a proof of those properties.

No. “Multi-shot borrows” refers to borrowed access associated with computation that can be resumed repeatedly. Repeating that computation must not create a new owner each time. The proposal distinguishes the ability to resume from the ownership claim and uses guards to account for borrowed access while a resumption is active.
Why does the proposal need ranked suspended handles if active resumptions already have guards?

An active guard concerns borrowed access during a running resumption. A suspended handle concerns a continuation that is not currently running but may still matter to future borrowed use. Ranking addresses dependencies among those suspended handles; guarding an active resumption addresses a different state. Neither component simply substitutes for the other.
Does “ranked” mean there is a fixed limit on how often a handle can be resumed?

Not as stated. The rank describes a constraint on suspended-handle dependencies, not a count of allowed resumptions. The proposal does not set a numerical resume limit. Its aim is to support multi-shot use while keeping the relevant ownership and lifetime constraints coherent.
Would the handle rank itself protect a borrow during execution?

No. Ranking a suspended handle and guarding an active borrow have distinct jobs. A rank constrains how suspended dependencies can be arranged; an active-resumption guard represents the borrowed dependency while a resumption is running. A ranking cannot be treated as if it were the protection needed by an active borrowed use.
Why call the finalizers owner-handle-free rather than simply guard-free?

“Owner-handle-free” expresses the specific relationship the proposal excludes: a finalizer retaining a handle guarded by the owner it is supposed to finalize. It does not state that finalizers can never encounter any guard or handle whatsoever. Keeping the description narrow matters because the proposal needs active guards to continue protecting live borrows.

Not necessarily. The proposal expressly calls for deferred exactly-once cleanup. Keeping a finalizer free of its owner's guarded handle removes one possible obstruction to cleanup; it does not, on its own, define the exact moment finalization takes place. Cleanup still has to respect any borrowed access that remains live.
What does “deferred” add to “exactly once”?

“Deferred” concerns timing: cleanup should not invalidate borrowed computation that is still permitted to run. “Exactly once” concerns the owner's obligation: cleanup must neither be omitted nor performed twice. Waiting can address premature cleanup, but merely waiting is not enough if the owner can remain unfinalized indefinitely. The combined proposal needs an account of both timing and occurrence.

No. Several active guards can express several outstanding borrowed dependencies on the same owner without multiplying that owner. Their purpose is to keep live borrowed uses from being invalidated, not to grant independent rights to finalize the resource.

Cancellation is a situation in which cleanup and borrowed access can interact sharply. The proposed combination must ensure that cancellation does not cause deferred finalization to invalidate a borrow in an active resumption. It must also avoid leaving cleanup permanently blocked by the suspended-handle or finalizer relationships it admits. The proposal does not spell out a complete cancellation transition or claim that all such interactions have been proved safe.

The proposal does not say so. Ranking constrains their structure, while any rule that ends their protection would still need to respect permitted uses and active borrows.
What does an active-resumption guard need to preserve when a handle changes from suspended to running?

It needs to preserve protection for borrowed access during the active computation. The transition must not leave a permitted resumption using a borrow whose owner has become unavailable. The proposal identifies both suspended handles and active guards, but does not specify the exact transfer or acquisition rule at that transition.

That is not established by the restriction alone. Owner-handle-free finalizers address one kind of dependency that could impede cleanup.
